summary: Log skidding with a horse and leading a horse on foot (scripts/horse/horse_haul.gd, skid_load.gd, log_pile.gd, horse_lead.gd). A felled tree's bole (limbed and topped when it is chained) or a bundle of logs from the pack is dragged on a chain from a singletree behind the horse; the pull it takes caps the horse's speed. Every number here is a design value (basis D) and tunable.
basis: Friction: a log skidded end first on forest litter and soil, roughly 0.4 along it and about twice that across it (design values; forestry figures for ground skidding run about 0.4-0.7, far less on snow). Pull: a horse works all day at about a tenth of its weight, and for a short heavy pull leaning into the collar it can start one to one and a half times its weight (pulling-contest practice); the speeds fall between those. Green wood weights are approximate figures after the USDA Wood Handbook's green weights, from memory and not checked against the table in this workspace.

pack_log.note: gathering.json items.log: an 8-foot length of trunk; the pack does not know its tree, so a bundle is taken as pine of this size

carcass.note: Dead animals dragged on a rope round the neck, head first (scripts/horse/carcass_load.gd). Friction: hair on forest litter, a little less with the lie of the hair than across it (design values). Weights: rough whole-animal live weights of the eastern woodland animals, from memory and not checked against a source in this workspace: a whitetail doe about 55 kg, a buck about 80 kg, an eastern wolf about 35 kg, a red fox about 6 kg.

foot.note: Dragging a dead animal on foot (scripts/horse/foot_drag.gd; user 2026-09-27: dragging on foot, a torch in the other hand): a short rope from the left hand to the loop round its neck, walked forward. The pull (the carcass friction above, and the slope) caps the walker: a fox at a jog, a wolf or a doe at a slow walk, a buck slower; past max_kgf nothing is refused (user 2026-09-27: 'make it where it is extreme slow'): the pace falls as max_kgf / pull toward extreme_mps. Design values (basis D): a man drags a whitetail out at about a slow walk, and leaning into a rope can hold perhaps 40-60 kgf for a short pull.

foot_log.note: Pulling a log on foot with both hands, walking backward (scripts/horse/log_pull.gd; user 2026-09-27: drag fallen trees, a log barricade). The log's friction is the horse's (mu_axial, mu_lateral above) and the pull caps the pace: at easy_kgf a little over the source pull clip's own step (0.52 m/s back), at max_kgf a crawl; past it nothing is refused (user 2026-09-27: 'make it where it is extreme slow'): the pace falls as max_kgf / pull toward extreme_mps. GAME VALUES, not a man's real pull (perhaps 60-90 kgf for a short heave): the forest's trees run 0.25-0.39 m in radius (p10-p90; median 0.31), so one 2.4 m length of a middling white pine, birch or maple is 280-420 kg, and max_kgf lets one person crawl such a length along (about 425 kg at mu_axial 0.4); a hemlock's or an oak's, or a whole trunk, goes at an extreme crawl (the horse is far quicker).

wheelbarrow.note: The wheelbarrow (scripts/horse/wheelbarrow.gd; user 2026-09-27: 'wheel borrows where we can use to add items in so instead of dragging if the has a wheel borrow it can be faster'). The pace by the load in it (kg, piecewise between the pairs; past the last, slower still as last_kg / load, down to extreme_mps): empty at a jog, a doe (55 kg) at a brisk walk, faster than dragging her (about 1.1 m/s), a log length slower. Design values (basis D): a man wheels 100 kg on a level path at a walk; the wheel takes the weight, so what is hard is balance and ground, not the pull. Weights of the pack's things (kg a unit) for the pace; the pack itself is not weighed yet.
